Content:
Whenever we add two complex numbers [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2,] we sum their real and imaginary parts. Geometrically, the real and imaginary parts of [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] can also be interpreted as components of two-dimensional Cartesian vectors.

Content:
In this sense, the addition of complex numbers is done component-wise (the same as vectors), and we can thus use the parallelogram law to add complex numbers geometrically.

Content:
To illustrate, let's look at the argand diagram for [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a7ba76f907e357d36cdf574e17027e70]

Content:
The sum of the two numbers (vectors) is obtained by placing them head to tail and drawing an arrow from the first tail to the last head.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4e8a92caad8a9f13982f97957411d32d]

Content:
Vector addition works in precisely the same way.

Content:
How do we plot the product of two complex numbers in the complex plane?

Content:
First, let's assume that [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] are expressed in polar form:

Content:
[MATH: z_{1}|= r_{1}(\cos θ_{1} + \textrm{i}\sin θ_{1}); z_{2}|= r_{2}(\cos θ_{2} + \textrm{i}\sin θ_{2})]

Content:
As we know, the product [MATH: z_1\cdot z_2] is given by the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: z_3 = z_1\cdot z_2 = r_1 \cdot r_2\left( \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \textrm{i} \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\right)]

Content:
This formula reveals some vital information:

Content:
- The modulus of [MATH: z_3] equals the product of the moduli of [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \vert z_3 \vert = \vert z_1 \cdot z_2 \vert = \vert z_1 \vert \cdot \vert z_2 \vert = r_1\cdot r_2 ,]
- The argument of [MATH: z_3] equals the sum of the arguments of [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \arg(z_3) = \theta_3 = \theta_1 + \theta_2]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Sum of Two Complex Numbers as Vector Addition

Content:
Whenever we add two complex numbers [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2,] we sum their real and imaginary parts. Geometrically, the real and imaginary parts of [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] can also be interpreted as components of two-dimensional Cartesian vectors.

Content:
In this sense, the addition of complex numbers is done component-wise (the same as vectors), and we can thus use the parallelogram law to add complex numbers geometrically.

Content:
To illustrate, let's look at the argand diagram for [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a7ba76f907e357d36cdf574e17027e70]

Content:
The sum of the two numbers (vectors) is obtained by placing them head to tail and drawing an arrow from the first tail to the last head.

Graphic:

Vector addition works in precisely the same way.

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Product of Two Complex Numbers in the Complex Plane

Content:
How do we plot the product of two complex numbers in the complex plane?

Content:
First, let's assume that [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] are expressed in polar form:

Content:
[MATH: z_{1}|= r_{1}(\cos θ_{1} + \textrm{i}\sin θ_{1}); z_{2}|= r_{2}(\cos θ_{2} + \textrm{i}\sin θ_{2})]

Content:
As we know, the product [MATH: z_1\cdot z_2] is given by the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: z_3 = z_1\cdot z_2 = r_1 \cdot r_2\left( \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \textrm{i} \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\right)]

Content:
This formula reveals some vital information:

Content:
- The modulus of [MATH: z_3] equals the product of the moduli of [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \vert z_3 \vert = \vert z_1 \cdot z_2 \vert = \vert z_1 \vert \cdot \vert z_2 \vert = r_1\cdot r_2 ,]
- The argument of [MATH: z_3] equals the sum of the arguments of [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \arg(z_3) = \theta_3 = \theta_1 + \theta_2]

Content:
Let's see an example.
